results.description:
This poster was designed by Chris McBride and Barney Pikari with the illustration by D P Witehira. It advertises Merata Mita's political film Patu!  Mita brought together film of the violent clashes during the Springbok rugby tour protests in 1981.

The Springbok Tour was a seminal event in New Zealand's political and social history - exposing deep rifts in society. Many New Zealanders objected to the tour because of South Africa's policy of racial apartheid. Protests caused obstruction and the cancellation of games, and violence escalated between protesters, supporters and police during the tour.Many people saw the tour as an opportunity to address racism in New Zealand. Māori protestors challenged non-Māori New Zealanders over the double-standard of fighting apartheid in South Africa instead of racism and deep-seated injustices here.

results.description:
This poster advertises the final leg in a march against unemployment led by Te Roopu Rawakore o Aotearoa.
The march began in Te Hapua, New Zealand's most northerly settlement (which was also the starting point for the 1975 Maori Land March).
Te Roopu Rawakore O Aotearoa was a national movement established in 1985 to encompass the many unemployed and beneficiaries’s groups throughout New Zealand. Members used protest actions to educate the government and public that unemployed workers were dispossessed workers not dole bludgers; unemployment caused poverty; unemployed workers deserved the right to organise in unions; and some groups in society were more likely to experience unemployment because of discrimination.
Labour historian Cybèle Locke notes that ‘unemployed workers’ unions were organised non-hierarchically and used Maori cultural processes to build the movement. They adopted a bicultural structure to share power and resources equally between Maori and non- Maori unemployed and beneficiaries in the movement’ (Workers in the Margins, 2012, p. 78).

results.description:
This poster protests against the South African government’s ‘honorary whites’ policy which enabled All Black Bryan Williams to tour South Africa with the All Blacks in the 1970s. Williams (born 1950, New Zealand) is of Samoan descent.
Until the All Black tour of South Africa in 1970, the New Zealand Rugby Union had bowed to South Africa’s apartheid laws and racist policies by sending the All Blacks without Māori and Pacific players, regardless of mounting protest pressure from many New Zealanders.
Background
Protests were voiced from the very first meeting of the South African and New Zealand rugby teams in 1921 when the Springboks visited New Zealand. When the Springboks played the New Zealand Māori team, a South African journalist's racist report published in South Africa was re-published in New Zealand papers, insulting Māori and supporters.
When the All Blacks made their first tour of South Africa in 1928, Māori players were not included. When the Springboks returned to New Zealand in 1937, Arawa iwi sought a social and sporting boycott of the tour. In 1949, despite protests, Māori players were not considered for the tour of South Africa. 
However, it wasn’t until the proposed 1960 All Black tour of South Africa that a wider protest movement arose (called the ‘No Maoris No Tour’). Two years of protests – including a massive petition, lobbying of government and direct action in the streets – brought the issue before all New Zealanders, but did not prevent the tour from going ahead.
In 1970 and 1976 protest demonstrations continued to play out in the streets as the All Blacks left to tour South Africa.
Sir Bryan Williams
Bryan Williams was only 19 when he debuted with the All Blacks and travelled to South Africa on the 1970 tour. He was the first Pacific player to represent New Zealand in rugby (three Māori players also went - they were all treated as 'honourary whites'). He went again to South Africa with the All Blacks in 1976 (five Māori players were included - again all were considered 'honourary whites').
After his playing career, Williams went on to coach Samoa. In 2018 Williams received a knighthood for his services to rugby and was inducted into World Rugby’s Hall of Fame.
In a 2018 interview with Rugby Pass, Williams commented on his participation in the 1970 tour to South Africa. He considered himself to be socially engaged as a law student, and personally believed he was making a genuine stand against apartheid. Reflecting on his involvement: ‘…I guess it was only in later life that you realise the significance of it. It just created a small dent in the armor of apartheid that they were willing to accept four of us as the first coloured players to go to South Africa, and that had some impact down the line’ (https://www.rugbypass.com/news/in-conversation-with-sir-bryan-williams/).
Rona Bailey
This particular poster belonged to activist Rona Bailey (1914-2005) who first became involved in protests against apartheid in South Africa from the late 1940s, and campaigned against the 1960 All Black tour of South Africa. For most of the 1970s, Bailey worked full-time and voluntarily for the anti-apartheid movement. Te Papa holds her hard hat worn during Springbok rugby tour protests in 1981 (GH011699).

results.description:
Small poster with an arrangement of text giving details of the entertainment provided by a Māori troupe at a "Māori Village" located at Clontarf pleasure gardens in Sydney, Australia, circa 1909 to 1911. Troupe is described as "the Whakarewarewa Maoris of 60 performers - men, women, and girls - under the management of Maggie Papakura. Performances daily at 3 and 8.30 p.m". 
Various entertainments are listed in English and te reo Māori including: "Tableaux, The Maori at home...Appearance of distinguished visitors Powhiri raurakau...Whaikorero (address of welcome by the chief"; songs, poi games "Tirairaka and Poi Paretireti"; matemate "a catch game"; haka, an "English part-song"; titi torea "ancient game of the Māori played with sticks"; and two further poi games performed and designed by Guide Bella and featuring canoe-building and a canoe poi dance. The final item was a "war cry Ka mate! Ka mate! Kia kutia". 
The Maori village at Clontarf, Sydney, opened in December 1909, as the venue for performances by Te Arawa Troupe under Maggie Papakura. The troupe performed there for two seasons 1909-1910 and 1910-1911 until the group left for England in March 1911. The village contained a carved wharenui, pataka, whare, and two waka taua which were transported by ship from New Zealand. results.description:
This 'Tāhae 250' poster counteracts Tuia – Encounters 250, the New Zealand government’s nationwide programme of events intended to celebrate Aotearoa’s Pacific voyaging history while commemorating the 250th anniversary of the first collisions between Māori and Captain James Cook and the Endeavour crew in 1769. Many copies of the poster were pasted up around Wellington streets in November 2019 to protest the visit of the replica Endeavour ship to the capital from 30 November to 3 December.
Activists dubbed it the 'death ship'. With its weapons of war and military crew, HMB Endeavour exacted a violent and deathly toll on indigenous populations. Nine Māori were killed by Cook’s men when they visited Aotearoa in 1769.
Tāhae means thief, cheat, robber, crook, theft, and dispossession. Many felt that the government did not fully realise ‘the depth of ill-feeling towards the arrival of Cook from a Māori perspective’ (Moera Brown quoted in The Spinoff, 5 October 2019), and the problems of an event largely promoting a Pākehā history. This poster challenged the official commemorations by reminding viewers of the ideology of white supremacy underpinning 'discovery' and its commemoration.

results.description:
This poster was designed by members of Te Roopu Rawakore O Aotearoa who collaborated with Wellington Media Collective (WMC) to produce the poster as they were not trained artists or printers. This was in line with the WMC’s philosophy: 'we will work with you, but not for you' (1979).
Te Roopu Rawakore O Aotearoa was a national movement established in 1985 to coordinate the many unemployed and beneficiaries groups throughout New Zealand at that time. Members used protest actions to educate the government and public that unemployed workers were dispossessed workers not dole bludgers; unemployment caused poverty; unemployed workers deserved the right to organise in unions; and some groups in society were more likely to experience unemployment because of discrimination.
Labour historian Cybèle Locke notes that ‘unemployed workers’ unions were organised non-hierarchically and used Māori cultural processes to build the movement. They adopted a bicultural structure to share power and resources equally between Māori and non-Māori unemployed and beneficiaries in the movement’ (Workers in the Margins, 2012, p. 78).
